title: Vayelech: write this song (Deuteronomy 31:19)
hookLine: the Torah's last command is to write it; the Talmud says each Jew should write a scroll (Sanhedrin 21b)

lines: NOT A SIGNATURE, NOT A LIST.
YOU CAN'T SKIM WITH A PEN.
cards: When did you last write something out by hand that you didn't have to? Not a signature, not a shopping list: copying words because they mattered. A pen slows you down, and you can't skim with a pen.
Every letter gets a moment. Almost at its end, the Torah gives a commandment about writing. By the traditional count, it's the last commandment in the whole Torah.

teach.b: God tells Moses: "Now therefore write ye this song for you, and teach thou it the children of Israel." Plainly, the song is the poem that comes next, Ha'azinu, which we'll begin in two days.
But the rabbis read the verse more widely. The song, they said, means the whole Torah. And write ye means every person.
In the Talmud, in Sanhedrin, the teacher Rabbah says: even if your parents left you a Torah scroll, it's a commandment to write one of your own.
Maimonides counts this among the six hundred thirteen commandments, and in the Torah's order it comes last. Writing a full scroll by hand is the slow work of a trained scribe, a sofer.
So how does an ordinary person do it? Some commission a scribe.

teach.h: ONE LETTER, GUIDED BY THE SCRIBE.
teach.b: In some communities, when a new scroll is nearly finished, people take turns filling in a letter, with the scribe guiding the hand.

And some authorities, like the medieval sage known as the Rosh, taught that in later times writing or acquiring books of Torah study carries the same spirit. Underneath is a plain idea: inheriting isn't enough.
The tradition wants each person to make it their own, letter by letter. This week we walked from Nitzavim into Vayelech. You can return.
Very near. Choose life. He went to them.
Strong and of good courage. Everyone gathers.

how: A Torah scroll is written by hand by a trained scribe (sofer) on parchment; communities often celebrate the completion of a new scroll by letting members fill in its final letters, guided by the scribe.

o: and he wrote: the scroll Moses finishes
and he sang: the song Moses teaches
and he went: the name of this short portion

games.q: inside the last commandment — tap the pairs.
p: even if you inherit a scroll, write one
read by the rabbis as the whole Torah
helping to finish a new scroll

s: inheriting a Torah scroll from your parents fulfills the commandment
Rabbah: write one of your own.
by the traditional count, it's the last commandment in the Torah

games.q: your grandparents left you a beautiful Torah scroll. according to Rabbah in the Talmud, what's left for you to do?
games.why: Sanhedrin 21b: even if your ancestors left you a scroll, it's a commandment to write your own.

practice: If you can, find a pen and paper; if not, trace the letters with a finger on your palm or on the table.

Choose a line that's stayed with you this month, maybe choose life, or the word is very nigh unto thee, and copy it slowly, one letter at a time. Notice where your hand hesitates, and a word you'd never really looked at before.

wordCard.voice: Vayelech. And he went. And in it, the last commandment: write this song. Write your own.

orig.note: Hebrew: song. 'write ye this song', Deuteronomy 31:19.

carryVoice: Your line: write your own. Inheriting isn't enough; it becomes yours letter by letter. Day five hundred twenty-five.
